chunks: And from him, from al-Husayn, from Safwan, and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn al-Mughira, from Ibn Bukayr, who said:

Hamza ibn Humran married the daughter of Bukayr. When he intended to consummate the marriage with her, they said to him: 'We will not give her to you unless you swear an oath to us.' They did not accept from him an oath of manumission (al-'itq) because he did not consider it significant, but rather said: 'Swear to us by the zihar of your mothers and female slaves.' So he performed zihar from them. Then he mentioned that to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: 'There is no blame upon you, so return to them.'

If it is said: 'How can you say that zihar is not effective as an oath, while hadiths have been narrated stating that the expiation (kaffarah) is not obligatory except after the breach (hinth)? If zihar by the oath were not effective, the expiation would not be obligatory, neither with the breach nor without it.'

key_terms.اَلظِّهَار: Zihar (declaring one's wife like one's mother's back)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Zihar when performed as an oath to satisfy family conditions, and does it require expiation?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the juristic nuance in Imam al-Sadiq’s (AS) ruling on Zihar as a conditional oath (*yamin*), where the husband swore by the 'backs' of his mothers and concubines to satisfy his in-laws. The Imam’s declaration that 'there is no blame on you' highlights the Shia view that this specific formulation constitutes a valid oath rather than a formal divorce declaration, thereby distinguishing it from the standard Zihar that triggers the expiation (*kaffarah*) outlined in Surah al-Mujadila. This reflects the broader Shia legal principle of interpreting oaths literally unless explicitly linked to the ritual of divorce.
